title: Einstein Probe May Have Caught a Black Hole Swallowing a White Dwarf
summary: On July 2, 2025, the China-led Einstein Probe space telescope was conducting a routine sky survey when it spotted something extraordinary: an X-ray source that flared to incredible brightness, then faded by a factor of more than 100,000 over 20 days. What made this event, designated EP250702a, truly bizarre was its timing. About a day before NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detected gamma-ray bursts from the same location, Einstein Probe had already recorded steady X-ray emission. That sequence — X-rays first, then gamma rays — is the reverse of what's seen in typical gamma-ray bursts, where a brief, intense flash of gamma rays precedes an X-ray afterglow. “This early X-ray signal is crucial,” said Dr. Dongyue Li of the National Astronomical Observatories of China, lead author of the study published in Science Bulletin. “It tells us this was not an ordinary gamma-ray burst.” The Einstein Probe's two instruments were key. The Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT), with its novel lobster-eye optics, first detected the source and provided a precise location. The Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) then monitored the event as it evolved, revealing a shift from hard (high-energy) to soft (low-energy) X-rays. Ground-based telescopes pinpointed the source to the outskirts of a distant galaxy, far from the central supermassive black hole where most high-energy events originate. After evaluating multiple scenarios, the international team — including researchers from the University of Hong Kong — concluded that the most plausible explanation is an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) tearing apart and accreting a white dwarf. IMBHs, with masses between 100 and 100,000 suns, are a long-sought missing link between stellar-mass black holes and the supermassive behemoths at galactic centers. If confirmed, this would be the first direct observational evidence of an IMBH disrupting a white dwarf. The event's extraordinary peak luminosity — about 3 × 10⁴⁹ erg per second — ranks among the brightest instantaneous outbursts ever recorded. The unusual sequence of X-ray and gamma-ray emission may reflect the complex physics of a white dwarf being shredded: as the stellar remnant approaches the black hole, tidal forces could strip away its outer layers, producing X-rays before the final plunge triggers a gamma-ray burst. The discovery opens a new window into the population of elusive intermediate-mass black holes and their feeding habits. Follow-up observations are ongoing to search for any lingering emission and to better constrain the black hole's mass.
why_it_matters: This event bridges two extremes of black hole science: we know tiny ones and giant ones, but mid-sized black holes have hidden in plain sight. Finding them helps complete the picture of how galaxies and their central engines grow, and may explain where some of the universe's brightest flashes come from.

background_read: The Einstein Probe, launched in January 2024, is a joint mission of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the European Space Agency, and the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, designed to catch sudden X-ray flashes in the universe.

NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope has been scanning the sky for high-energy gamma rays since 2008. Astronomers have long sought 'intermediate-mass black holes' as the missing link between stellar-mass black holes (from collapsing stars) and the supermassive giants at galaxy centers.
A white dwarf is the Earth-sized, dense leftover of a sun-like star that has exhausted its fuel. When one gets too close to a black hole, extreme gravity shreds it.

perspectives.description: Astronomers celebrate a possible breakthrough in identifying IMBHs, a long-sought class, using innovative X-ray timing. The Einstein Probe's wide-field vision proved crucial in catching the early X-ray signal.

The interpretation is still provisional; alternative explanations, such as a peculiar stellar explosion, cannot yet be ruled out without more data. Some scientists may question whether the reverse sequence truly requires a black hole disruption.

The reversed sequence challenges standard models of gamma-ray bursts and forces a rethinking of how black holes feed on stars. It highlights how little we know about the population of mid-weight black holes.

With more such events, astronomers could build a census of IMBHs and understand their role in cosmic evolution. Next-generation X-ray telescopes may regularly catch similar disruptions, turning a rare discovery into a common tool for mapping the invisible universe.
